![](articleshare.jpg)

A wonderful [podcast from The Gradient](https://thegradientpub.substack.com/p/steve-miller-will-ai-take-your-job) I listened to on my late-afternoon run along the Lake Union today: host [Daniel Bashir](https://danielbashir.com/) interviews Professor [Steven Miller](https://accountancy.smu.edu.sg/faculty/profile/9608/Steven-MILLER) on the brave new world of AI and its impact to jobs. Steve is Professor Emeritus of Information Systems at [Singapore Management University](https://www.smu.edu.sg/), founding dean of the SMU School of Computing and Information Systems, and co-author with [Tom Davenport](https://www.tomdavenport.com/) of *[Working with AI](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262047241/working-with-ai/)* (MIT Press, 2022) — the 29 case studies referenced throughout the conversation.

**Key takeaways from the interview**:

- [**Augmentation is different from automation**](#ch-augmentation-vs-automation). We should strive for automating for the sake of augmentation ("bicycle for the mind").

- [**Comparing census 1940 to 2018, 60% of job titles are brand new**](#ch-real-world-difficulties).

- [**The labor question is about *what* work, not *how much***](#ch-real-world-difficulties). 11 of 12 largest economies project labor *shortages*, not surpluses. The real risk is failing to create new middle-income work as automation absorbs older work.

- [**Compared to machine intelligence, humans excel at contextualization**](#ch-human-machine-intelligence) — and the same strength injects *noise* into repetitive decisions. Algorithms outperform humans on consistency where consistency is what's wanted (Kahneman, Sibony & Sunstein, *Noise*).

- [**Organizational friction to adopt the latest tech may not be bad**](#ch-org-adoption) — it provides necessary brakes before we fully understand their implication. Complementary investments to make AI productive in an org are typically 4–10× the direct tech spend. Tech problem is ultimately a human problem.

- [**"Safe to speed"**](#ch-safe-to-speed). Better brakes let cars go faster. Responsible AI isn't the constraint on progress — it's what *enables* speed. Boeing's 737 MAX MCAS deployment is the cautionary counter-example: progress driven dangerously, not safely.

**My take:**

- Labor displacement may happen in targeted sectors (as always), but overall technologies will enable humanity to venture into new problem spaces, and the universe is infinite!

- Humans' contextualization advantage over machines may hold until a real embodied AI emerges.

- [Model explanation is a MUST for the era of human-AI collaboration, even at the cost of accuracy](#ch-tradeoffs). A lot of research in AI and HCI is needed.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Postscript (May 2026).** The displacement-vs-complement debate Steve sketches here resurfaced in finance-side form three years later: see [the Citrini Research / Citadel Securities 2028-crisis exchange](/posts/20260502-2028-intelligence-crisis/), where Citadel's rebuttal leans directly on Steve's "recursive capability does not imply recursive adoption" framing and on the same Microsoft-Office complement-not-replacement case the 29 *Working with AI* case studies documented.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The reference is to William Lee's stocking-frame knitting machine, invented circa 1589. The often-quoted line attributed to her ("Consider thou what the invention could do to my poor subjects…") is a later rendering, and the historicity of the specific exchange is uncertain — but the patent denial itself, and the anti-displacement reasoning, are well-documented.

But the world does change. New issues do come up. It's not just new technology, but new technology in particular does new kinds of things to different extents at different scales with different economics.

It is dominated by choices made in the deployment.

#### Choices in deployment, not technology, drive labor outcomes

### 11:35 — Automation and augmentation, and integrating new technologies in the workplace {#ch-augmentation-vs-automation}

#### The 29 *Working with AI* case studies — every one was augmentation, not automation

**Steve Miller:** So let's come to the theme of automation and augmentation. I'm not going to say "versus." I'm going to explain why I say "and."

And as you know, Daniel, I just published this co-authored book with the prominent co-author Tom Davenport, who for decades has been writing about trends in corporate IT and going back to the 80s, and then analytics, and then into AI. And it was a beautiful experience to be able to sort of work under the tutelage of Tom because he's such a master in story crafting.

And we did these 29 case studies. And we purposely chose successful deployments of AI-enabled solutions in a wide range of real-world work settings.

Nothing could be R&D. Nothing could be trial. 

Everything sort of had to be real, everyday work at that level. 

And they were all examples of augmentation. 

All right. A wide range. So one point to take away from that is there's more opportunities for augmentation. And I'm going to explain what I mean by augmentation versus automation in a moment. Then people realize we don't always have to default to the only alternative is full automation.

#### Definitions: automation drives wages down, augmentation drives output (and eventually wages) up

So let me come back to a stylized way in which labor economists and economists of technological change define automation and augmentation in a generalized way. Use of the word automation for when the deployment of the technology results in the person being made redundant. All right.

So an augmentation where the deployment is such that certain tasks or subtasks are automated, but the person is not made redundant. And in fact, the technology is used to complement and to increase the output and productive capability of the person.

So in the case of automation, the people doing that kind of work, their wages are driven down. In the case of augmentation, the people doing that kind of work, their output is driven up. And over time, hopefully, and usually the trend is their wages are driven up as well.

All right. Although there might be a lag there because in a sense they're contributing more.

Automation obviously creates job opportunities for the tenders, the designers, the people in the outer loops, if you will. But in the direct sense of the people doing that job, it drives down the wages. So the book had a lot of rich examples of augmentation. You hear a lot about displacement. You don't see a lot of case studies about complementarity.

Now, this is not to say that there are not examples of using automation and using increasingly capable automation via AI enablement for displacement. Obviously, you're going to have that. But it's to say there's more examples of augmentation than people realize.

#### Why augmentation works: the model can be good, not perfect — humans handle the long tail

Now, one of the big questions is, is that an intermediate stepping stone and holding point? Or is that going to be a persisting situation. And one of the reasons augmentation works so well is you just have more interplay in the sense that the technology can be good, but it doesn't need to be perfect.

And the combination of the person with the oversight, doing the adaptation, dealing with some of the error situations, you just have a lot, you can deal with a lot more and you can deal with contingencies.

And as any of you who build [ML](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_learning) [machine learning] models know, you can get them pretty reasonable in a not so long period of time. But that last 10%, that last 5%, that last 3% actually can be extraordinarily difficult, if not prohibitively expensive, and maybe not just worth it. And of course, when you have high transaction rates, a 10% or 7% error rate, 

you're dealing with these items all the time, right? So I have views on which we're going to see both. We're going to see some of the examples we had in the book, I predict, will stay as augmentation. Some will move beyond. And as the system gets better and the totality of the work experience gets more finely tuned, because it's never just the AI system, it's the surrounding process, higher degrees of automation will come in.

But what I think will happen, Daniel, is here's the thing most people don't fully appreciate. Even though with computers, 

increasingly more capable software, everything we can do with the marvels of modern machine learning makes our automation more adaptable…

Certainly compared to the way controls were done in software through logic, both with information systems and physical automation systems 10 years ago, 20, 30 years ago.

There's still a boundary that you're designing it.

And you can, with more capable, adaptive sensing, all of that, you can deal with a wider envelope of uncertainty, but the world just has this way of changing beyond your convenient little envelope of uncertainty. So there's always, always — and it's never going to go away — be that aspect of work where the nature of the adaptation, the nature of the pivoting, the nature of the changing, the nature of the need to explore, experiment, just goes beyond what the automation systems are designed for.

#### The double helix: stable regimes want automation, unstable regimes want augmentation

And automation systems really work best in not perfect environments, but relatively more stable, predictable environments where you need to scale, get consistency, repeatability, reliability. And economically, it's not A or B. You need both. You need those regimes of relative stability where I need to turn out the transactions more consistently, more productively, lower cost, where we want the automation.

But if that's all you're doing you'll never make the big changes, you're only transitioning the new things — and I don't mean just in the R&D lab, I mean in the production and operational parts of the company it's too — they're always doing things that are less familiar.

So there's always this sort of, you know, I think of it as a double helix or, you know, like a [Möbius strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6bius_strip) or a yin-yang thing between the simultaneous need for adaptability and for efficiency and productivity.

So that has implications for where we can fully automate and where we're going to use the AI-enabled tools for augmentation and support and enhancement.

And it's never going to go all one way or the other. We're going to retain with that simultaneity.

#### Distribution shift, in ML terms

**Daniel Bashir:** The adaptability component of what you just said is really important.

And connecting this to another conversation I had, if I can make this less understandable, 

is I think putting it in a way ML people might be familiar or used to thinking about it. When I spoke to [Zachary Lipton](https://www.zacharylipton.com/), this professor at CMU, he often speaks about, again, the ideas of things like [distribution shift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_adaptation).

So in kind of reintroducing this idea for listeners, in ML models, there are often assumptions that need to be made about where the data that you trained on comes from. And you often assume that the data you test on, the data in the quote real world, comes from the same place.

And Lipton often says that this is kind of just like, well, if you imagine this process over time, it's like your theoretical model is basically God decided to drop your data out of the sky on day one, and God decided to drop data in the exact same way on day two. And that's not at all how the real world works.

**Steve Miller:** No, exactly. And interestingly enough, there are regimes of economic activities where I want to buffer from changes in the environment.

You know, I've got this product, I've got this service. People want it in a predictable, reliable way. And I want it steady, steady, steady, right? And everything I want to do is to keep variation out of it, right? Which is a fabulous way to use automation to enhance consistency.

And while that part of the sort of economic revenue cycle is going, there's the simultaneous part that I want to do something that's different than what anyone else is doing. I want to do it in a different way. I want to do it in a way where we don't have prior data on. The customer doesn't have prior experience on. You know what I mean? How do you run the big ML in that kind of world? You don't.

So in that kind of thing, you'll use AI-based tools to help with experimentation, exploration, collaboration. But it's going to be a while before you can grow into the familiarity and be able to stabilize sort of a way of working where we can tune up the automation.

So the key thing is implied in the word of automation is doing what we're familiar with. It means doing today's work and yesterday's work, right? And that's important, but it's sort obvious that if that were always the case, we wouldn't be where we are in 2022, approaching 2023, relative to 1960, 1970, 1980. Somehow a lot of things, new things, new products, new services, new ways have to come in.

So yes, the technology will increasingly be used to automate, but automation is of the familiar and what you're trying to stabilize in a way and sort of milk the money out of and eventually it will wind down — but it's much harder to drive that automation in the less familiar. And every one of you just think about your everyday working experience and — you know, I don't mean sort of like the most deep esoteric research labs. I mean, sort of the everyday regular ways of work.

### 21:50 — Difficulties of applying AI systems in real-world contexts {#ch-real-world-difficulties}

#### Familiar work vs. new work in your everyday job

**Steve Miller:** Some things are familiar, steady, keep the variation out. And some things we're trying to figure it out.

You know, we're pivoting, we're changing, we're adapting, we're experimenting.

#### The Autor study: 60% of 2018 jobs were in titles that didn't exist in 1940

And that type of work, interestingly enough, tends to be very labor intensive. And just so the audience understands, I admire greatly the work of some of the economics of technology economists like [Erik Brynjolfsson](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/people/erik-brynjolfsson/) [[fix: Eric → Erik]] and [David Autor](https://economics.mit.edu/people/faculty/david-h-autor) [[fix: Alter → Autor]] at MIT and [Daron Acemoglu](https://economics.mit.edu/people/faculty/daron-acemoglu) [[fix: Darren Asimoglu → Daron Acemoglu]] at MIT. And there's, of course, many others, and they do fabulous work.

David Autor and a team of people from several other institutions, they looked at the employment in the U.S. in 1940. It was about 50 million people.

They took what they had at the time of their analysis was over the last two or three years, and U.S. employment data as of the end of 2018.

And it was 161 million people.

So in that 78 years, 1940 to 2018, you can just imagine everything that happened in the realm of technology. I mean, it was the age of the transistor, the age of the computer, the age of software and, you know, the age of the Internet. And you have it all there. Right. And yet employment increased from 50 million to 161 million.

Now, they did this thing, which was an estimate. 

And admittedly, it's an imperfect estimate because it's something that's impossible to know precisely. And their ability to do this estimate would have been impossible without modern natural language technology support for doing economic analysis, interestingly enough, because they looked at job titles from the census every few years, starting 1940, 50, 60, you know, all the way to 2010 and the latest data from 2018. And they looked at patent data and a whole bunch of other things.

And they made an estimate of that 161 million in the newer contemporary era. What fraction of it was in job titles that to the best that they could surmise, you know, the best analysis they could do, were job titles that existed in 1940 — versus what fraction of that total employment was in job titles that had been added to the census since 1940.

Now, remember, if there's only like nine of something in the country, it doesn't get added to the census. Something has to be prevalent enough where it shows up enough on enough radar screens where it gets added to the census.

And what they estimated is about 60% of the total amount of work in 2018 was in precise job titles that did not exist in 1940.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The figure traces to David Autor, Caroline Chin, Anna Salomons, and Bryan Seegmiller, ["New Frontiers: The Origins and Content of New Work, 1940–2018"](https://economics.mit.edu/sites/default/files/inline-files/Autor%2C%20Chin%2C%20Salomons%2C%20Seegmiller%202022.pdf) [[2]](#ref-2) (NBER WP 30389, Sept 2022; later QJE 2024). The headline summary is that "roughly 60 percent of employment in 2018 is found in job titles that did not exist in 1940" — Steve's number is on point.
:::

#### Labor shortage, not labor surplus, is the looming demographic problem

**Daniel Bashir:** Wow.

**Steve Miller:** So the point there is the importance of new work. Let me restate that again, the importance of new work. And when we talk about automation, we're almost always talking about existing, prior, somewhat more familiar, therefore older work. So we'll get the automation, you know, we'll use the technology for automation. That doesn't worry me.

The issue is, do we maintain the momentum of creating new types of work, new types of jobs, you know, and some obvious types of things. Creating ML solutions itself is its own little ecosystem of doing that.

New energy installation for solar or for battery systems or electric charging infrastructure is related to that. What's going on in pharma? Not all new work, by the way, is technology-driven. Some of it's services, right? Some of it's driven by taste, preferences, demographics, things like that. But the technology-driven new work tends to be higher skill, higher wage.

The things that, okay, now we have people who will paint nails or do tattoos or even like a [Grab](https://www.grab.com/) driver, it's new work. Some of it's not technology-enabled. Some of it is — like the [Uber](https://www.uber.com/) driver. Here we call it Grab, but it tends to be lower wage.

And in a nutshell, what — not all but some — very knowledgeable labor economists believe is that the issue is not going to be the number of jobs. In fact, as you see in the U.S. now, there's a shortage of people.

In 11 of the 12 largest economies in the world, because of demographics, the high proportion of the growth of older people at a faster rate than the growth of younger people, there's projected labor shortages in 11 of the 12 of the world's largest economies going out.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The "11 of 12 largest economies" framing is a heuristic Steve cites repeatedly across his work; the underlying source is typically [UN World Population Prospects](https://population.un.org/wpp/) projections combined with national labor-force participation trends. The exact ratio depends on which economies you include and the projection horizon — directionally true for 2030 and beyond, less crisp than the round number suggests.
:::

So labor shortage isn't the issue. It's the quality of the jobs. And of course, we're going to have the high-end jobs and the high-skilled jobs. Undoubtedly, we have, we will, but they'll continue. But will there be enough of those middle-income jobs? Will even the jobs on the lower end of the wages be sustainable and okay enough for people to live.

And all of those issues, when you state it like that, that's not a function of machine learning algorithms. It's a function of how people choose to deploy them and what they use to do.

And whether they're going to put focus on just automating the existing jobs and the jobs of yesterday and driving labor out. And even greater degrees of variation is judges who are supposed to be identically trained take essentially the same kind of case or an identical evidence base and rule differently.

A lot of these examples are explained in that book by [Daniel Kahneman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Kahneman) [[fix: Danny → Daniel]], [Olivier Sibony](https://www.oliviersibony.com/) [[fix: Oliver Sibonyi → Olivier Sibony]], and [Cass Sunstein](https://hls.harvard.edu/faculty/cass-r-sunstein/) called [*Noise*](https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/daniel-kahneman/noise/9780316451406/) [[3]](#ref-3), which I cannot recommend strongly enough.

Everybody doing the ML work, who's the gradient community, and even if you're beyond the gradient community, this is a must read.

It's not like the newest theory on the block. These folks working on this book have been doing this work for decades. And it reflects the craftsmanship and insight of decades of distillation.

But getting down to distilling sort of a thick book, noise in the way they define it is variability of a type that you don't want to be there.

#### Where you want consistency vs. where you want variability

When you're doing creative brainstorming sessions and certain facets of work and certain facets of your life, you want all kinds of unexpected variability. But when you're applying for a mortgage or when you go in to have the doctor look at your sore throat or, you know, you have a parking violation or, you know, you have to go to the justice system in some ways…

you'd like to see a certain consistency. We'd all like to see a certain consistency in here are the facts of the case. Here's what the judgment should be.

And what they show is that humans, for all the wonderful things that they do with reading context and contextualizing and seeing the special nature of each situation, that for certain kinds of decisions that especially are more repetitive like decisions, but not only repetitive decisions, inject noise into the process. Noise being defined here as undesirable types of variation.

So we have the ability to contextualize things and to customize, often to great and important effect. and we have the simultaneous ability when we're working in a certain kind of transactional mode and we all work, you know, different parts of our work, certain aspects of transactional mode to inject noise into the process in ways that would be better off if they're not there.

#### Algorithms (even simple ones) outperform humans on consistency

And they review the evidence that any kind of algorithm will perform more consistently than a human in certain kinds of decision tasks.

Doesn't have to be an ML thing. It could be a simple rule and then simple equal-weight regressions, which aren't always the most accurate answer, but actually they're very robust against changes in data distributions.

And then more finely tuned regressions.

And then, of course, ML takes it even to a higher level of consistency and accuracy. So this notion, and it comes back to this automation–augmentation thing.

When do we want to automate the decision process for stability and consistency? And when do we want the individualized, contextualized nature where we know we're injecting noise and variability, but that's okay.

And they describe some processes where, like you dimensionalize things, you evaluate them on each dimension, you have people do that independently, then you bring it together and have the social discussions to sort of figure out how to put people's ideas together. So how to combine that human capability with a certain kind of consistency, which undoubtedly machines, including algorithmic-based decision making — doesn't even have to be ML algorithms — help us do.

This is a new age. I mean, the problem's not new. There's variants of this that go back decades, but it's now, we've never had it at this scale before. And of course, the balance will be very contextualized and it will be evolutionary as a work unit or a process is sort of evolving. This is a kind of intelligence that we need humans to map out and to know where and how we use our machines so that we can get people to work competitively, to create value so we can pay them well.

And I don't think the answer is [universal basic income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_basic_income). I think it's the way we work. That's why it's so important these issues be worked out in every organization, small, medium, large, public sector, private sector, people sector.

**Daniel Bashir:** I think that's a perfect message for us to close out on. So, Steve, thank you for articulating that. I think that this is a really important set of questions for people both in the AI sphere, but also working in technology or frankly, anything more broadly to be thinking about. And I really appreciate your work, both the work you've done with us at The Gradient as well as your other writing.

And I want to thank you for doing all of that and for spending the time to talk with me today.

**Steve Miller:** Keep up that wonderful work with The Gradient and the fact that a small team does what they do and you serve the public interest and you guys do the fantastic articles and podcasts. It gives a ray of hope and it just shows there is a better side to our human nature.

And thank you for all the work you guys support.

### 1:09:41 — Outro {#ch-outro}

**Daniel Bashir:** And that is a wrap, my friends.

As I mentioned at the start of the episode, you can subscribe to The Gradient on Substack to receive not just this podcast, but also our articles and newsletters directly to your email.

You can also visit us at [thegradient.pub](https://thegradient.pub/), where you'll find all of that, as well as more information about The Gradient and how you could even contribute if you're interested.

And finally, if you enjoyed this episode, we would really appreciate your feedback.

If you'd like to leave a comment or review, we'd love to know how we can make this series more interesting and informative to you.

And with all that, I'll leave you until the next episode.
